entry: [[Pharaoh]] of [[Ancient Egypt]] and founder of the Eighteenth Dynasty. His reign is usually dated to the mid-16th century BC, at the beginning of the Late Bronze Age. He completed the conquest and expulsion of the Hyksos, restored Theban rule over Lower and Upper Egypt, and reasserted Egyptian power in [[Nubia]] and [[Canaan]]. He reorganized the administration, reopened quarries, mines and trade routes, and began a building program that culminated in the last pyramid built by native Egyptian rulers. His mother, Ahhotep, served as regent during his minority. Manetho credited him with abolishing human sacrifice to [[Hathor]] at Heliopolis. His reign laid the foundations of the [[New Kingdom of Egypt|New Kingdom]], under which Egyptian power reached its peak.

Principal god and sky deity of [[Zoroastrianism]]. The words Ahura and Mazda literally mean “lord” and “wisdom”. In the Yasna, he is the first and most frequently invoked spirit. Some Zoroastrian historians hold that his worship predates [[Zoroaster]]. The first notable invocation of Ahura Mazda came in the Behistun Inscription of [[Darius the Great]] during the Achaemenid period (c. 550–330 BC). Until the reign of Artaxerxes II he was invoked alone in royal inscriptions; under Artaxerxes II he was grouped in a triad with Mithra and Anahita. Images of him appeared from the 5th century BC, but under the Sasanian dynasty an iconoclastic movement replaced them with stone-carved figures and then removed them entirely.

City on the Karun River, capital of Khuzestan province, Iran. Its metropolitan area has over 1.3 million people, including Persians, Arabs, Qashqai and Kurds. Ahvaz lies near the border with [[Iraq]]. The Karun, the largest river in Iran by volume, flows through the city, which has been known as the City of Bridges and, since the beginning of the 20th century, as the Oil Capital of Iran along with other cities of Khuzestan province. The settlement dates to the Achaemenid period, when it was called Taryana and lay on the Royal Road from [[Persepolis]] to Sardis. Under Ardashir I it was renamed Hormazd-Ardeshir, later abbreviated to Darawashir. In ancient times it was one of the main centers of the Academy of Gondishapur.

American serial killer. Working as a street prostitute along Florida highways in 1989–1990, she robbed and killed seven men who picked her up. She initially testified that the first victim had raped her, and in a 2001 court petition she wrote that robbery was the motive in all seven deaths. A jury convicted her of the murder of Richard Mallory in 1992. After more than ten years on death row, she was executed by lethal injection. Her life has been the subject of an opera and of *Monster* (2003).

Indigenous people of northern Japan and southeastern Russia, living mainly on [[Hokkaido]]. Japanese assimilation policies from the Meiji period onward forced many Ainu off their land and banned their religion and language. The Hokkaido Ainu language is likely extinct, with no known native speakers. Official surveys in Hokkaido received 11,450 responses in 2023, while unofficial estimates in 2002 placed the total population in Japan at 200,000 or higher, because many people of Ainu descent do not know their ancestry. In 2019 Japan’s Diet passed the Ainu Policy Promotion Act, which formally recognized the Ainu as indigenous.

Flag carrier of India, headquartered in Gurugram, Haryana. The airline is owned by Air India Limited, which is held by the [[Tata Group]] (74.9%) and [[Singapore Airlines]] (25.1%). Founded in 1932 as Tata Airlines by J. R. D. Tata, it was nationalized in 1953 and later renamed Air India. It took delivery of its first [[Boeing 707]] on February 21, 1960, becoming the first Asian airline to introduce a jet aircraft. Control returned to the Tata Group in 2022, after 69 years of government ownership.

Removal of heat from an enclosed space to achieve a more comfortable interior temperature, and in some cases control of humidity. Mechanical units typically use vapor-compression refrigeration, while passive and ventilative cooling are alternative methods. [[Heat pump|Heat pumps]], which use a reversing valve, can both heat and cool a space. In hot weather, air conditioning can prevent heat stroke and other hyperthermia-related harm, and an estimated 190,000 heat-related deaths are averted annually. The International Energy Agency counted 1.6 billion air conditioning units worldwide in 2016. As of 2022, air conditioning used about 7% of global electricity and emitted 3% of greenhouse gas. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptian]] buildings used passive techniques, which fell out of fashion in the 20th century. Willis H. Carrier designed the first modern electrical unit in 1902, to stabilize humidity in a [[Brooklyn]] printing plant.

National military branch that primarily conducts [[Aerial warfare|aerial warfare]], distinct from army or naval aviation. Air forces typically gain control of the air, carry out strategic and tactical [[Bomber|bombing]], and support land and naval forces with reconnaissance and close air support. Many also command air defense assets such as [[Surface-to-air missile|surface-to-air missiles]]. The first aviation force was the Aviation Militaire of the French Army, formed in 1910. The Royal Air Force, founded on April 1, 1918 by amalgamating the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service, is generally regarded as the first independent air force. Arguably, the Finnish Air Force, formed on March 6, 1918, was first. Air forces rely on many non-pilot specialties, including logistics, intelligence, maintenance and cyber support.

Large body of air defined by its temperature and [[Humidity|humidity]]. Air masses take on the characteristics of the surface beneath them and are classified by latitude and by continental or maritime source region. Continental air is dry, while maritime and monsoon air is moist. Weather fronts separate air masses of different density. The Bergeron classification, the most widely accepted scheme, uses three letters. The first gives moisture (c for continental, m for maritime). The second gives the source region (T tropical, P polar, A arctic or Antarctic, M monsoon, E equatorial, S for air dried and warmed by downward motion). The third gives stability (k if the air is colder than the surface, w if warmer). Thus cP denotes a cold, dry continental polar air mass.

Presence in the air of substances harmful to humans, other living things or the environment. Pollutants include gases such as ozone and nitrogen oxides, and particles such as soot and dust. Outdoor pollution comes mainly from burning [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuels]] for electricity and transport, [[Wildfire|wildfires]], industry, waste management and agriculture. Indoor pollution often comes from burning firewood or agricultural waste for cooking and heating. Air pollution kills 7 to 8 million people each year and is a significant risk factor for [[Stroke]], heart disease, [[Asthma]] and [[Lung cancer]]. The World Bank has estimated that welfare and productivity losses from air pollution cost the world economy over $8 trillion per year. The Montreal Protocol almost eliminated harmful ozone-depleting chemicals.

Scale estimating current or forecast [[Air pollution|air pollution]] levels, rising as pollution rises. Countries use their own versions, such as Canada’s Air Quality Health Index, Malaysia’s Air Pollution Index and Singapore’s Pollutant Standards Index. The U.S. scale runs from 0 (good) to 500 (hazardous). At high levels, governments typically advise children, the elderly and people with respiratory or cardiovascular problems to reduce outdoor activity.

Ground-based service that directs aircraft to prevent collisions and expedite air traffic. Controllers use [[Radar]] and [[Radio]] to enforce separation rules that keep a minimum distance between aircraft. Pilots must obey instructions, but the pilot in command keeps final authority and may deviate in an emergency. Croydon Airport near London introduced air traffic control in 1920. After the 1956 Grand Canyon mid-air collision killed all 128 people on board, the Federal Aviation Administration was given air traffic responsibility in the United States in 1958. In 2001 the [[European Union]] aimed to create a “Single European Sky” to boost efficiency. Under International Civil Aviation Organization rules, operations are conducted in English or the local language, and English must be used on request.

American online marketplace for short- and long-term homestays and experiences. Founded in [[San Francisco]] in 2008 by Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia and Nathan Blecharczyk, it began as AirBed & Breakfast, offering air mattresses to conference visitors, and the name was shortened in 2009. Airbnb charges a commission on each booking. It expanded to [[Cuba]] in 2015 after the easing of U.S. restrictions. Critics argue that short-term rentals reduce long-term housing supply and raise rents, and some analyses find the effects modest or context-dependent.

Airborne radar system that detects distant threats and directs friendly fighters. AEW&C aircraft can detect aircraft from up to 400 km (220 nmi) away, beyond the range of most [[Surface-to-air missile|surface-to-air missiles]]. One aircraft at 9,000 m (30,000 ft) can cover 312,000 sq km (120,000 sq mi). The [[Northrop Grumman]] E-2 Hawkeye is assigned to U.S. Navy supercarriers. AWACS is the name of the system on the [[Boeing]] E-3 Sentry, and is often used as a general synonym for AEW&C.

First twin-engine widebody airliner and first production aircraft of [[Airbus]]. Airbus Industrie GIE, the consortium that developed it, was formally created on December 18, 1970. The A300 prototype first flew on October 28, 1972, and launch customer Air France introduced the type on May 23, 1974. Production ran from 1971 to 2007, with 561 deliveries. The A300 typically seats 247 passengers. As of December 2025, 209 A300 family aircraft remained in commercial service.

Family of single-aisle twinjet airliners made by [[Airbus]]. The A320 program was launched in March 1984, first flew on February 22, 1987, and entered service with Air France in April 1988. Variants include the A318, A319 and stretched A321. The re-engined A320neo entered service with Lufthansa in January 2016 and offers up to 15% better fuel economy. The family pioneered digital fly-by-wire and side-stick flight controls in airliners and is the best-selling airliner ever built.

Full-length double-deck quadjet airliner and the world’s largest passenger airliner. [[Airbus]] flew its first prototype on April 27, 2005. Electrical wiring problems delayed production by two years, and the first delivery went to [[Singapore Airlines]] on October 15, 2007. Production peaked at 30 aircraft a year and ended in 2021. The estimated $25 billion development cost was not recouped. Typical seating is 525, with a maximum certified capacity of 853. As of April 2024, there were 189 aircraft in service with 10 operators.

European aerospace corporation that became the world’s largest airliner manufacturer in 2019. Airbus Industrie GIE, a consortium formed in 1970 to compete with American airliner makers, was merged into EADS in 2000; EADS was renamed Airbus SE in 2015. Its divisions also cover defense and space and helicopters. The company is legally headquartered in Leiden, Netherlands, with its main office in Blagnac, France. In 2020 it reached a global settlement exceeding $3.9 billion over bribery and corruption in aircraft sales. Trade disputes with [[Boeing]] over government subsidies have produced World Trade Organization rulings against both companies.

Warship designed to carry, launch, recover and support aircraft at sea. Its full-length flight deck and hangars make it a mobile airbase, and it is usually the capital ship of a carrier battle group. Since [[World War II]] the carrier has replaced the [[Battleship|battleship]] as a fleet’s flagship. Carriers are among the largest warships because they need ample deck space, and they must be fast, at more than 30 knots to evade nuclear submarines. Operating in international waters, a carrier does not need land-use authorization from third-party countries. The United States operates 11 large nuclear-powered carriers, each carrying around 80 fighters. [[Henry Kissinger|Henry Kissinger]] called an aircraft carrier “100,000 tons of diplomacy.”

Power component of an aircraft propulsion system. Most aircraft engines are piston engines or gas turbines, though a few have been rocket powered and many small UAVs use [[Electric motor|electric motors]]. Developing a jet engine takes around eight years and billions of dollars or euros, and the last successful entrant to the global jet engine market was [[General Electric]] in the 1970s. Five European and American manufacturers dominate the market as of 2025. Engines are typically sold at a loss, and manufacturers profit from maintenance services and parts over a lifespan of roughly thirty years. In 2020 the Pipistrel E-811 became the first electric aircraft engine awarded a type certificate by EASA.

Company that provides regular air transportation of passengers or freight. Airlines use aircraft and operate under an air operating certificate or license from a government aviation body. DELAG, founded on November 16, 1909, is considered the world’s first commercial passenger airline; it operated [[Zeppelin]] airships from June 1910 until 1935. A fixed-wing scheduled airline began in the United States in January 1914, flying between St. Petersburg and Tampa, Florida. Ownership moved from mostly personal to government control from the 1940s to 1980s, then back to large-scale privatization. Since the 1980s, mergers and alliances such as Star Alliance, SkyTeam and Oneworld have expanded codesharing among airlines. Airlines carried approximately 4.4 billion passengers in 2023.

1980 American comedy film that parodies disaster films. Written and directed by David Zucker, Jim Abrahams and Jerry Zucker, *Airplane!* borrows the plot of *Zero Hour!* (1957) and stars Robert Hays, Julie Hagerty and Leslie Nielsen. Released by Paramount Pictures, it grossed $171 million worldwide against a budget of $3.5 million. Its writers won the Writers Guild of America Award for Best Adapted Comedy. The film is known for surreal humor and fast-paced slapstick, and it was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry in 2010.

Fixed-wing aircraft propelled by a jet engine, propeller or rocket engine. The [[Wright brothers]]’ Wright Flyer, flown in 1903, is recognized as “the first sustained and controlled heavier-than-air powered flight.” George Cayley set out the concept of the modern airplane in 1799. The German Heinkel He 178 was the first jet aircraft, in 1939, and the [[De Havilland Comet]], introduced in 1952, was the first jet airliner. The [[Boeing 707]] was in commercial service from 1958 to 2019. Commercial aviation transports more than four billion passengers a year. In American English the aircraft is called an airplane; in most of the Commonwealth it is an aeroplane.

Aerodrome with extended facilities, mostly for commercial air transport. Its landing area includes at least one operational surface, such as a runway or helipad, and it often has control towers, hangars and terminals. Larger airports for airline flights generally have paved runways of 2,000 m (6,600 ft) or longer. Alberto Santos-Dumont coined the word in a 1902 interview with [[The New York Times]]. In U.S. usage, an airport is a landing area regularly used by aircraft to receive or discharge passengers or cargo. As of 2009, the CIA counted about 44,000 airports or airfields recognizable from the air worldwide, including 15,095 in the U.S. Airports are major employers, but they are also large sources of [[Air pollution|air pollution]] and noise.

Powered lighter-than-air aircraft, also called a dirigible. Airships rise on a lifting gas less dense than air. Early airships used [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]], whose flammability caused fatal accidents, and most built since the 1960s use non-flammable [[Helium|helium]]. Non-rigid airships, or “blimps,” keep their shape through gas pressure alone. Rigid airships, often called [[Zeppelin|zeppelins]], have an internal framework and were mostly built by the firm of Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin. Airships were the first aircraft capable of controlled, powered flight, but their decline accelerated after the 1937 explosion of the hydrogen-filled Hindenburg. Since the 1960s, helium airships have been used for advertising, tourism and aerial observation.
